title: Who is Cletis Tout?t??
full_review:
In order to save his life, an escaped convict must "pitch" the story of how he came to assume the identity of Cletis Tout, a marked man, to a movie-obsessed hit man in writer-director Chris Ver Weil's oddball romantic comedy "Who is Cletis Tout?" (Paramount Classics).

Humorous tongue-in-cheek references to Hollywood give this film its idiosyncratic tone, but the borrowed characters and plot devices, as well as flat performances by the film's leading actors, weigh down the otherwise sensitive love story.

Funnyman Tim Allen stretches his acting muscles by playing Critical Jim, the film-quoting hit man obsessed with Hollywood. He's hired to kill mob snitch Cletis Tout, but instead of finding the real Tout, he finds Trevor Finch (Christian Slater), an escaped convict who has assumed Tout's identity. In a bid to save his life, Trevor offers to tell Critical Jim the story of how he came to assume Tout's identity. He appeals to Jim's fondness for films by proclaiming that his story, like a great film, has it all: a jewel heist, a prison break, a pretty girl.

Trevor has 90 minutes to "pitch" his story "Hollywood style" before Jim decides how it's going to end. As Trevor narrates, Jim constantly critiques him as if he were the president of a film studio about to make the story into a movie -- hence the name Critical Jim. He also recites lines from classic films like "The Maltese Falcon" and "Double Indemnity," while pining for the days when movies were driven by character, not special effects.

"Who is Cletis Tout?" is loaded with references to other films. Some, like the ones Jim recites, are obvious, but others may slip by undetected. Jim himself shares some traits with Leon, the main character in Luc Besson's 1994 film "The Professional." Both characters are hit men who love to watch "Singin' in the Rain." It's a charming device for softening the tough exterior of a hit man, a way to make them seem more human, but Allen doesn't need softening. His portrayal of a hit man is far more subdued than the rampaging Leon character.

The most provocative and bizarre dialogue in the film is a debate between two hit men about the homosexual themes in John Boorman's troubling 1972 film "Deliverance." This conversation is very similar to the pointless arguments between two other hit men in Quentin Tarantino's ultra-violent 1994 drama "Pulp Fiction."

Portia de Rossi plays Tess, the daughter of Micah (Richard Dreyfuss), Trevor's friend who escaped from jail with him. Micah hid millions of dollars worth of diamonds in a field just before he was sent to jail, and now that he and Trevor have broken out, the duo, along with Tess, scheme to retrieve the diamonds. However, thanks to hit men, mobsters, police looking for Cletis Tout and some other unforeseen glitches, retrieving the diamonds is going to take some ingenuity.

At first, Tess despises Trevor, but romance begins to bud between the two as they are forced to work together to retrieve the diamonds. Slater and de Rossi make an unexpectedly endearing on-screen couple, which may be, in part, due to the fact that there is nothing sexually gratuitous about their relationship. It is sweet and innocent throughout the whole film. Rare it is that two attractive actors with an on-screen relationship don't jump into bed by film's end.

However, the film does have a few lurid subplots. RuPaul plays a sleazy cross-dresser who comes on to Trevor (thinking he's Tout, of course). He passes along to Trevor a copy of an incriminating tape, meant for the real Tout (who filmed it), which jarringly shows a high-ranking mobster strangling a girl during an intense sexual encounter. This tape is sought by the mob and the police, thus making it the reason Tout is such a wanted a man.

Due to an intense sexual encounter, brief nudity, recurring violence, disturbing images of corpses, some homosexual references, and sporadic rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
